clue.text: Reasons to sell singular titanium parts

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, so one piece is pushed apart to take another inside

parts.note: a shop that moves stock sells it
Ti is the chemical symbol for titanium
S is the grammar abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A metals trader explains why they are selling off titanium parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' looks like a noun for components, but it is a verb: the selling word is split to take in the metal, and the singular sign follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Motives are the underlying causes that lead someone to act, a close synonym of reasons.

clue.text: Cruise perhaps tipped to win Oscar? Doubtful

indicators.note: tipped up in a down entry, so the word is tilted over and read from the bottom
to win something is to take it and hold it, so one piece gains another inside itself

parts.note: Tom Cruise is an example of someone called Tom
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Is the actor Tom Cruise really favourite to win an Academy Award? Unlikely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipped' pretends to mean 'predicted to win', as a favourite is tipped; here it flips the name. 'Perhaps' marks Cruise as one example of a Tom.
explanation.definitionFit: A moot point is open to argument and unsettled, so the adjective means debatable or uncertain.

clue.text: His tour unfortunately misses one Scottish town

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the letters end up in a bad, jumbled order
to miss something is to go without it, so a letter is left out of the fodder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one, which is removed

explanation.surface: Someone's trip around Scotland goes badly and skips a town on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the I out of HIS TOUR and rearrange the six letters that remain. Thurso is a town on the far north coast of Scotland, in Caithness.
explanation.definitionFit: Thurso is a real town in the Highlands, the most northerly on the British mainland, so it is an example.

clue.text: Of diverse tastes, one keeping unconventional home?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: having free-ranging, unconventional artistic tastes
second meaning: a person who lives in an irregular, arty household

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves describe the same free-living artistic type, first as an adjective and then, with the question mark marking a playful angle, as a noun for the person.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Bohemia, once thought the homeland of wandering Romani people, and now describes artists living outside social conventions.

clue.text: After it comes sweet decision

parts.note: surface reading: once something is over, a pleasant choice follows
setter's reading: the choice of pudding follows one stage of a meal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' reads as an adjective meaning pleasant, but it is the British word for dessert: after this part of dinner you decide on pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal dish of a meal is followed by dessert, when diners choose what sweet they would like.

clue.text: Escort having space to climb without resistance to find carnivore

indicators.note: climbing in a down entry means going upward, so the letters are read from the bottom
in its old sense without means outside, so these letters sit around another

parts.note: to escort someone somewhere is to take them
an em is a printer's space
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A guide with room to climb, and no resistance, sets off to track down a predator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without resistance' reads as 'unopposed', but 'without' is the old word for outside: the reversed letters wrap round R. An em is a printing space the width of the letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: The meerkat is a small African mongoose, a member of the order Carnivora, eating insects and small animals.

clue.text: Name fish with unusually hot stuffing

indicators.note: stuffing is what fills the inside of something, so these letters go inside another

parts.note: the dory is an edible sea fish

indicators.note: something done unusually departs from the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Christen a fish dish that comes with an unusually spicy stuffing.
explanation.walkthrough: The recipe picture is the misdirection: the fish is literally stuffed with the rearranged heat word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy is a woman's first name, so it is one example of a name.

clue.text: Old female performer bored by comedian

indicators.note: to be bored is to have a hole drilled through you, so one piece has another driven into it

parts.note: a doer is one who performs an action
a wag is a joker or wit

explanation.surface: An aging actress is bored stiff by a stand-up comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' reads as weary, but it means drilled into. 'Performer' suggests an actor; here it is simply one who performs, a doer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow holding a title from her late husband, and the word is used loosely for any dignified elderly woman.

clue.text: Polite chap lagging each trunk is tree expert

indicators.note: lagging is insulation wrapped around a pipe, so one piece wraps round the others

parts.note: a gent, short for gentleman, is a well-mannered man
ea is the abbreviation for each
a log is a section of tree trunk
taken as written

explanation.surface: A courteous man is wrapping up tree trunks, as a forestry expert might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lagging' reads as falling behind, but it is the lagging that wraps pipes. The trunk and tree suggest forestry, yet the tree here is a family tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A genealogist researches family history and draws up family trees, so the definition plays on the arboreal sense.

clue.text: Step in plant root to be picked up

indicators.note: a sound picked up by the ear is heard, so we go by how the words are spoken

parts.note: to inter is to put in the ground, as one plants; seed is what takes root

explanation.surface: An instruction for planting: set the root down in the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step in' looks like a gardening instruction, stepping into a bed, but it is the definition. Inter is to bury, and seed is sown to root.
explanation.definitionFit: To intercede is to intervene on someone's behalf in a dispute or trouble, a formal equivalent of stepping in.

clue.text: Geek's way to reach Tyneside from the south?

parts.note: Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in the North East of England
Rd is the abbreviation for road
surface padding linking the route to its destination
surface padding: travelling north up the road towards the region

explanation.surface: A train spotter describes the best route to Newcastle coming up from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: Coming from the south you head up to the North East along a road: the region is the destination and is named first. Tyneside is the Newcastle area of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Geek and nerd are both informal words for an obsessive, socially awkward enthusiast, often of computers.

clue.text: Uncertain yes/no taken to show lack of an essential principle to build on

indicators.note: something uncertain is not fixed, so the letters are not fixed in their order
to lack something is to be without it, so those letters are left out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A wishy-washy yes-or-no answer reveals someone with no firm principles.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A and N from TAKEN, then rearrange the remaining TKE with YES and NO.
explanation.definitionFit: The keystone is the central wedge stone locking an arch; figuratively it is the central idea everything else depends on.

clue.text: Wake from nightmare perhaps, losing head for time when trapped under lingerie

indicators.note: the first letter is lost and something else stands in its place
in a down entry, lying under means coming after, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: slips are women's underskirts
T is the abbreviation for time
a nightmare is a kind of dream, which loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Waking from a bad dream to find oneself tangled in underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake' reads as a verb for rousing from sleep, and the nightmare supports that; it is the noun, the disturbed water behind a boat. DREAM swaps its D for T.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipstream is the current of air or water behind a moving vehicle or vessel, much as a wake trails a ship.

clue.text: What balloonist might say about black line on weather map

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: a balloonist rising up might say 'I soar'
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: A balloonist comments on a black line they can see on the weather chart.
explanation.walkthrough: The balloonist's boast is I SOAR, which goes round B.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line joining places of equal atmospheric pressure, drawn on meteorological charts.

clue.text: Marking a long stretch away, having included lawyer's terms in email bust-up

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: by means aside or away, as in 'put by'

indicators.note: a bust-up is a violent quarrel that breaks things apart, so the letters are scattered
terms are limits or ends, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of lawyer
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawyer's clauses spark a furious email row over something long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away' gives the outer pair of letters, as in 'put by'. The answer nods to this puzzle being Toughie number 2,000, a bimillenary of sorts.
explanation.definitionFit: Bimillenary relates to a period of two thousand years, so it marks a very long span of time, such as a two-thousandth anniversary.

clue.text: Difficult to believe when credit's cut — or hard to swallow

indicators.note: to cut is to take something out, so letters are removed from the word

parts.note: incredible means hard to credit
CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit, which is removed

explanation.surface: A story is hard to accept once its credibility is cut, or simply hard to swallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to swallow' is usually said of an unbelievable story, which chimes with the first half; here it is literal, food that cannot be eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Inedible food is unfit or unpleasant to eat, so it is literally hard to get down the throat.

clue.text: One once associated with McEnroe leads to new racket being brought in?

definitions.text: One once associated with McEnroe leads to new racket being brought in?

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside, so these letters go within another word

parts.note: the actress Tatum O'Neal was married to the tennis player John McEnroe

indicators.note: leads are what go at the front, so only the first letters are taken

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: John McEnroe, famous for losing his temper on court, is linked to a noisy new racket.
explanation.walkthrough: N and R are slotted separately into TATUM. John McEnroe was a US tennis star notorious for outbursts at umpires, so the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: McEnroe's on-court outbursts were famous, so a childish fit of rage is the thing most associated with him, and it makes a racket.

clue.text: Brush with journalist in dropping-off place

indicators.note: in means inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: a broom is a long-handled brush
ED, an editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A brief encounter with a reporter at a drop-off point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brush with' reads as a near encounter and 'dropping-off place' as somewhere to leave things, but it is where you drop off to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off is to fall asleep, and a bedroom is the room where people go to sleep.

clue.text: Keeps individual out of old trouble

parts.note: to keep something is to have it

indicators.note: something out of the word is no longer in it, so that letter is removed

parts.note: sole means single or individual
O is the abbreviation for old, removed

explanation.surface: Someone stays clear of an old spot of bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps out of trouble' reads as one familiar phrase, but 'out of old' is the deletion and only the last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A hassle is an annoying difficulty or bother, an informal equivalent of trouble.

clue.text: Perhaps Mary's new green card not initially enclosed

indicators.note: not at the start means the first letter is dropped
something enclosed is shut inside, so one piece goes within another
a new version is a remade one, so the letters are made into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
the word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Mary's new US green card, the residency permit, has not been sent in the envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?' makes Mary a gardener; 'Perhaps' flags her as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary in the nursery rhyme tends a garden of silver bells and cockle shells, so she is an example of a gardener.

clue.text: Ease off runs with fast time around end of June

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so these letters go round another

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the month

explanation.surface: A runner eases off, clocking a quick time at the end of June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast time' reads as a quick time in a race, but it is a period of fasting. R and LENT together go around E.
explanation.definitionFit: To relent is to become less severe or give way, so it means to ease off or soften.

clue.text: Brilliant performer or, occasionally, soothsayer
Partners entering rituals regularly roll back barrier to passage?

indicators.note: entering means going into, so these letters go inside another piece
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
North and South are partners at the bridge table

indicators.note: going back means going the other way, so the word is read right to left

parts.note: a roll is a list, as is a rota

explanation.surface: Couples join in regular ceremonies, rolling back a barrier to let people through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll back' reads as one phrasal verb, but roll is a list and back reverses it. 'Passage' means the passing of heat or current, not a corridor.
explanation.definitionFit: An insulator is a material that prevents electricity, heat or sound from passing through it, hence a barrier.

clue.text: On the up, foxhunters appear to abound

indicators.note: going up in a down entry means reading from the bottom, so the word is flipped

parts.note: foxhunters gather at a meet; appear is 'meet' in the sense of assemble

explanation.surface: Hunting folk seem to be everywhere, and their numbers are rising.
explanation.walkthrough: A meet is the gathering of riders and hounds before a fox hunt, a very British tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: To teem is to be present in great numbers or to be full of something, so it means to abound.

clue.text: German artist on the rise, it's said, having lasting quality

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so the words are judged by how they sound

parts.note: Albrecht Dürer was a German painter; a bull is a trader expecting prices to rise

explanation.surface: A German painter's reputation is climbing, they say, because his work lasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rise' reads as growing fame, but it is market slang: a bull bets on rising prices. Albrecht Dürer was a Renaissance German artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Something durable withstands wear and survives a long time, so it has a lasting quality.

clue.text: Cover most of something that is pushed more than seemed possible

indicators.note: taking the greater part but not the whole means the final letter is dropped

parts.words: something that is pushed more than seemed possible
parts.note: to push the envelope is to go beyond accepted limits

explanation.surface: A cover story about going further than anyone thought possible.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'push the envelope', from test pilots exceeding safe flight limits, gives the thing that is pushed; its last letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop is to wrap up or surround completely, so it is a verb meaning to cover.
